analysis.one_liner: Turns Death Valley and Joshua Tree into national parks, creates the Mojave National Monument, and designates California desert wilderness.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 297-136, but the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings and never brought it to the Senate floor, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have converted Death Valley and Joshua Tree National Monuments into full national parks, added roughly 1.5 million acres as the new Mojave National Monument, and designated about 73 new wilderness areas plus millions of acres of park wilderness. It would have withdrawn those lands from mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal development, while continuing existing grazing until 2016 and preserving existing utility rights-of-way. The House passed it overwhelmingly, but the Senate committee never reported it, so it never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Americans who hike, camp, and visit the California desert gain permanently protected parks and wilderness; Native Americans gain guaranteed access for traditional cultural and religious uses; and future generations gain public wildlands shielded from mining and development.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes Death Valley National Park and Joshua Tree National Park, converting the existing monuments into full park units with enlarged boundaries to protect contiguous Federal lands from incompatible development [S2] [S3] [S4].
Creates the Mojave National Monument of approximately 1.49 million acres, replacing the impermanent East Mojave National Scenic Area, and permits hunting on its lands [S3] [S4].

Designates approximately 73 new wilderness areas on Bureau of Land Management desert land, plus roughly 3.18 million acres of Death Valley wilderness, 695,056 acres of Mojave wilderness, and Joshua Tree wilderness additions [S3] [S4].

Withdraws the park, monument, and wilderness lands from the mining laws, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, and bars the government from disposing of those lands or granting new rights-of-way in wilderness [S2] [S4].
Guarantees Native American access for traditional cultural and religious purposes, including temporary closures to protect the privacy of those activities [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Mining claim holders and companies lose access to land withdrawn from the mining and mineral leasing laws; grazing permittees keep current privileges only until July 1, 2016; and taxpayers fund land acquisition, a visitor center, and management of the expanded park system.

drawbacks.text: Existing grazing on park and monument lands is preserved at current levels until July 1, 2016, a quarter-century grandfathering for permit holders before all grazing ends [S2] [S4].

The military title reserves China Lake and Chocolate Mountain lands for Navy use, exempts the United States from liability for injuries from nonmilitary activity on those lands, and preserves low-level military overflights over the new parks and wilderness [S3].
The bill authorizes appropriations without a funding limit, and directs priority acquisition of ranchers' base property, leaving acquisition and management costs to taxpayers [S3] [S4].

Existing utility rights-of-way for Southern California Edison, Southern California Gas, and the Metropolitan Water District are preserved, and Edison's transmission lines may be upgraded in place through the monument [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large and durable: permanent national park and wilderness protection for several million acres of desert that the bill's own findings describe as threatened by development. The costs are comparatively narrow and largely transitional, borne by mining and grazing interests and by taxpayers for acquisition and management, though the 25-year grazing grandfather and preserved military overflights and utility corridors significantly soften the conservation result.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin in November 1991, but the Senate's Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings in 1992 and never reported the bill, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 17, 1991, with 87 cosponsors (81 Democrats, 6 Republicans), and referred to the House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee [S1] [S5] [S6].
The House Interior Committee ordered the bill reported 28-16 and reported it amended on November 4, 1991 [S6].
The House passed the amended bill on November 26, 1991, by a recorded vote of 297-136, with 251 of 267 voting Democrats in favor and 45 of 166 voting Republicans in favor [S7] [S6].
The Senate referred the bill to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and its Public Lands, National Parks subcommittee, which held hearings in California and in Washington in April 1992 [S6].

The Interior Department's executive comment was unfavorable in the House (October 1991) and again in the Senate (August 5, 1992); the committee never reported the bill, and it died at the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining claim holders, companies seeking desert mineral and geothermal access, and other development interests were better off, since the lands stayed open to the mining laws and multiple use for at least two more Congresses rather than being withdrawn and protected as parks and wilderness.

sides.party_line_note: Support split sharply by party: 251 of 267 voting Democrats (94%) voted yes while only 45 of 166 voting Republicans (27%) did, and the bill then stalled in the Senate committee.

industries.note: The bill withdraws park, monument, and wilderness lands from the mining laws, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, and requires validity review before any mining plan is approved. That forecloses private mineral extraction on lands the public uses for recreation and preservation.

Grazing continues at current levels for permit holders, but all grazing on Death Valley additions and the Mojave monument ends July 1, 2016. Ranchers get a quarter-century grandfather plus priority sale of base property to the government.

industries.industry: Electric and water utilities (Southern California Edison, Southern California Gas, Metropolitan Water District)
industries.note: The bill preserves existing rights-of-way through the new monument and parks and lets Edison upgrade transmission lines in place, locking in infrastructure that serves Southern California water and power customers.

industries.industry: Land development and Catellus Development Corporation
industries.note: Development of the protected lands is barred, but Catellus, a major private landholder inside the boundaries, gets a negotiated federal land exchange with an exchange account it can use to bid on surplus federal property.

Title VIII reserves China Lake and Chocolate Mountain lands for Navy training and weapons use for 15 years, exempts the government from liability for nonmilitary-activity injuries, and preserves low-level military overflights over the new parks and wilderness.
